summary: German has a real verb “to have”: haben. It is irregular in two forms – du hast, er/sie/es hat (the b disappears) – and otherwise regular: ich habe, wir haben, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben. What you have is the object of the sentence, in the accusative case (fully taught at S07): you can see it only with a masculine noun – der Bruder → Ich habe einen Bruder, mein Sohn → Ich habe einen Sohn; feminine, neuter and plural look the same as in the nominative (eine Schwester, ein Baby, zwei Brüder). haben is used for possession and family (Ich habe zwei Kinder) and for many states where English uses “be” (Hunger haben = to be hungry, Zeit haben = to have time). It is not used for age (Ich bin zwanzig) or for “there is” (es gibt).

blocks.title: Age is sein
blocks.text: Ich bin zwanzig (Jahre alt). – not *Ich habe zwanzig Jahre. German uses sein for age, like Greek (είμαι είκοσι χρονών) and English.

blocks.title: haben where English says “be”
blocks.text: Hunger haben (to be hungry), Durst haben (to be thirsty), Angst haben (to be afraid), Recht haben (to be right), Glück haben (to be lucky), Zeit haben (to have time).

blocks.title: “There is” is es gibt
blocks.text: Es gibt hier ein Café (there is a café here) – not *Hier hat ein Café. haben needs a person or a thing that owns something.

items.title: Greek and English
points: a verb “to have”, like German: έχω, have
both mark the object on a masculine article: Greek έχω έναν αδελφό, German Ich habe einen Bruder

items.title: Russian and Turkish
points: no everyday “have” verb: у меня есть брат (“at me there is a brother”), bir kardeşim var (“my sibling exists”)
Arabic and Hebrew work the same way (“at me”, “there is to me”) – German is the odd one out

askYourself: Who has it? → ich habe, du hast, er/sie/es hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie haben, Sie haben.
Am I saying it politely? → Sie haben (with a capital S).
Is the thing I have masculine and singular? → einen / meinen (Ich habe einen Bruder); otherwise the form does not change.
Am I saying someone’s age? → sein, not haben.
Do I mean “there is / there are”? → es gibt, not haben.
steps: Choose the form of haben for the subject.
Put what is owned after the verb.

traps: du hast, er hat – no b in these two forms.
Ich habe einen Bruder, not *ein Bruder: haben takes the accusative.
Age: Ich bin zwanzig, not *Ich habe zwanzig.
Sie haben = you have (polite) and they have – only the context and the capital S (inside a sentence) tell them apart.

quiz.why: der Bruder is masculine; after haben it is accusative: einen Bruder.
Feminine: eine stays eine in the accusative.
Polite Sie takes the plural form haben.

seeAlso.note: Arabic has no verb “to have”: it says “at me” – عِنْدِي (ʿindī), from the preposition عِنْدَ with a pronoun suffix.
Hebrew says “there is to me”: יֵשׁ לִי (yesh li); the negative is אֵין לִי (ein li).
Chinese uses the verb 有 (yǒu), as German uses haben; its negative is 没有 (méiyǒu), never 不有.
The accusative after haben (einen Bruder) is the direct object, taught fully at S07.
